newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan port workers to go on strike Wednesday.
newsitem.headline: Japan port workers to go on strike Wednesday.

text.p: Japanese port workers, angered by a U.S. decision to impose a $100,000 surcharge on Japanese ships, will stage a 24-hour nationwide strike from Wednesday morning to protest against the sanctions.
About 100 labour union members will gather at a Tokyo port for a rally to mark the strike, union officials said.
The stoppage is expected to disrupt operations at all major ports in Japan, including Yokohama and Kobe, shipping industry officials said.
Shipping firms have voiced concern that the strike would make it increasingly difficult to avert the U. S. sanctions, which would cost the industry an annual five billion yen ($41.3 million).
"We will take various measures to try to minimise the impact of the strike," a spokesman for leading ship operator Nippon Yusen KK said.

U.S. maritime authorities said last month they would slap a $100,000 surcharge on each Japanese vessel entering a U.S. port from abroad in retaliation for what it called unfair Japanese port practices.
The surcharges are to go into effect on April 14.
U.S. and Japanese officials met in Washington on March 3 and 6, but were unable to narrow their differences, a foreign ministry official said.

The dispute centres around U.S. charges that the Japan Harbour Transportation Association (JHTA) has put in place costly and discriminatory practices through a "prior consultation" system of negotiations and pre-approvals involving carriers, JHTA and waterfront unions.
Washington also says Japan's licensing requirements for terminal operators and stevedoreing firms discriminate against foreign firms.
The JHTA has shown no signs of relenting, prompting concern from Japanese shipping firms who say they are innocent victims in the dispute.
The JHTA is made up of port cargo-handling firms and serves as the mediator between unions and shipping companies.
The Japanese government has conceded that port practices are in need of reform but argues that the sanctions violate international agreements.

Shipping firms, both foreign and Japanese, together with the JHTA are to meet as early as next week in order to try to iron out differences and reach an agreement to reform port practices, the foreign ministry official said.
"It is unlikely the parties involved will reach an agreement easily," the official said.
Earlier this year, Japan's eight big ports announced plans to change their wharfage system from May in an attempt to boost international competitiveness.
The effect would be a decrease in fees for mooring up to 12 hours but an increase for a 24-hour stay.
